newsitem.title: FRANCE: Freeze is mixed blessing for French grain farmers.
newsitem.headline: Freeze is mixed blessing for French grain farmers.

text.p: Snow and ice is hampering grain deliveries in parts of France but the big chill has brought relief to some farmers whose crops are still in the ground, grain traders said on Friday.
A hard layer of frost in southern France allowed tractors into the few remaining fields where last year's maize crop still needed to be harvested, they said.
"There was a problem before Christmas with too much water on the ground," a leading maize trading specialist in southwestern France told Reuters.
"Now people have been able to take advantage of the cold weather and get the last few tonnes of maize in."
Further north, wheat farmers were relieved that the cold snap which descended on Europe about 10 days ago had brought rapid snow as the mercury plunged.
"There is a fairly good level of insulation from snow and we don't see many problems at this stage," said a trader in the Paris area, where much of France's autumn-sown winter wheat is grown.
Snow, which helps to protect crops from the worst effects of frost, arrived fairly quickly after the bitter temperatures first moved into the wheat belt at the end of December.
An official with France's ITCF technical grains institute said it was too early to say what impact, if any, the cold weather would have on winter crops.
But he said conditions were not excessive for this part of the cycle, when winter wheat was just beginning to sprout secondary shoots and only shallow snow cover was needed.
"These are temperatures which can certainly be tolerated," he said. "Just a few centimentres of snow will be enough to provide protection at this stage."
The Meteo France weather office reported more snow and rain in southern France on Friday, with localised patches of sleet.
The northern half of the country was said to be grey and cloudy with pockets of fresh snow.
Afternoon temperatures were four degrees Celsius below freezing point in the grain regions around the capital.
The record low for this time of year was 16.8 degress below zero in Janbuary 1985.
Grain traders said it was difficult to obtain a precise picture of the impact on prices, with most cooperatives and merchants still on a traditional two-week shutdown for New Year.
But demand for grain-based animal feed could be expected to rise as farmers kept more of their livestock indoors, they said.
With many canals iced up, and miles of railway line frozen, the main problem now was a logistical one, they said.
Rapeseed deliveries in the Moselle area, which depend heavily on waterways, were said to be among the worst hit.
"Just about everything on barges is stuck," one trader said.
